title: Proving the Line y = ex Is Tangent to y = e^x
originalTopic: Tangency between an exponential curve and a line through the origin
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: The line y = ex (where e is Euler's number) looks as if it just grazes the curve y = e^x. Find the point of contact, verify that the two graphs share a slope there, and explain why the plot shows no other intersection.
finalAnswer: \text{Tangent at } x = 1, \text{ point } (1, e); \qquad e^x \ge ex \ \text{for all } x, \text{ with equality only at } x = 1

steps.title: Check the shared point
steps.explanation: Both graphs have height e at x = 1, so (1, e) is a common point.
steps.why: Any tangency claim must first satisfy the value condition, otherwise the graphs merely run parallel.

steps.title: Check the shared slope
steps.explanation: The derivative of e^x at x = 1 equals e, exactly the slope of the line, so the line is the tangent line there: e + e(x - 1) = ex.
steps.why: Equal value and equal first derivative is the defining test for tangency of order one.

steps.title: Show the contact point is unique
steps.mathExpression: g(x) = e^x - ex, \quad g'(x) = e^x - e = 0 \Rightarrow x = 1, \quad g''(1) = e > 0
steps.explanation: The difference has its single critical point at x = 1, where it is a minimum with value g(1) = 0, so g(x) >= 0 everywhere and equals 0 only at that point.
steps.why: A nonnegative difference vanishing once proves the line never cuts the curve, ruling out hidden intersections outside the plotted window.

steps.title: Read it as an inequality on screen
steps.mathExpression: \text{window } [-2, 3] \times [-1, 10]: \ e^x \text{ hugs then rises above } ex
steps.explanation: In that frame the exponential touches the line at (1, e) and lies above it on both sides, shrinking toward 0 as x goes to negative infinity while the line descends.
steps.why: The picture is a visual proof of the tangent-line inequality for the convex function e^x: the graph always stays above any of its tangent lines.
